seatResponsibilities: Evaluate threats, privacy, security controls, continuity, recovery and crisis readiness.

criterionDimensions.name: Detection, incident response, and crisis readiness
Security governance, evidence, and continuous improvement

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I identify credible threat actors, motives, capabilities, access paths, and assets before selecting security controls.
I model abuse cases in addition to accidental failure so legitimate features cannot be exploited without scrutiny.
I map trust boundaries, entry points, privileges, data flows, and external dependencies for material systems.
I distinguish vulnerability, threat, exploitability, exposure, and business consequence when prioritizing security work.
I identify attack paths that combine several individually minor weaknesses into a material compromise.
I include insider, compromised-identity, supply-chain, automation, social-engineering, and physical scenarios when relevant.
I test assumptions about network location, device trust, identity strength, and administrative privilege rather than treating them as facts.
I model how an attacker could persist, escalate, exfiltrate, disrupt, manipulate, or destroy after initial access.
I prioritize threat scenarios by credible consequence and exploit path rather than headline fear.
I update threat models when architecture, data, users, integrations, or attacker capability materially change.
I identify information, systems, services, identities, facilities, and processes whose compromise would materially harm the organization.
I classify data according to confidentiality, integrity, availability, legal, contractual, and business requirements.
I distinguish critical business services from the technology components that support them.
I map dependencies required to deliver critical operations under normal and degraded conditions.
I define system and data owners who are accountable for protection requirements.
I identify crown-jewel assets whose compromise creates disproportionate financial, operational, legal, or reputational harm.
I establish retention and disposal requirements that reduce unnecessary attack surface.
I distinguish production, test, development, backup, archive, and analytical copies when assessing exposure.
I include credentials, secrets, keys, certificates, configurations, logs, and metadata as security-sensitive assets where appropriate.
I revisit criticality classifications when business use, regulation, architecture, or consequence changes.
I design identity as the primary security boundary when distributed systems make network location insufficient.
I apply least privilege to users, administrators, services, workloads, agents, and automation.
I separate authentication strength from authorization scope and govern both deliberately.
I use role, attribute, contextual, or policy-based access according to the decision being controlled.
I define joiner, mover, leaver, privilege-elevation, and credential-recovery processes with accountable ownership.
I protect privileged access with stronger controls, monitoring, separation, and time-bounded elevation where justified.
I reduce standing administrative privilege when temporary or just-in-time access can meet the operational need.
I govern service accounts, workload identities, API keys, secrets, and certificates through explicit lifecycle controls.
I design access reviews around material entitlements and business ownership instead of ceremonial recertification.
I ensure emergency access exists for resilience without allowing emergency paths to become permanent bypasses.
I choose preventive, detective, corrective, and recovery controls according to the threat and consequence they address.
I design defense in depth so one control failure does not automatically become catastrophic compromise.
I use secure defaults and deny-by-default boundaries where they materially reduce accidental exposure.
I segment systems and privileges according to trust, criticality, and blast radius rather than organizational convenience.
I protect data in transit and at rest with cryptographic controls appropriate to sensitivity and threat.
I design secure configuration, patching, vulnerability management, and hardening as lifecycle capabilities.
I include application security, dependency security, infrastructure security, and operational controls in one coherent design.
I define logging and telemetry needed to detect misuse without collecting unnecessary sensitive data.
I evaluate control effectiveness using evidence of the threat path it interrupts, not merely control presence.
I accept residual technical risk only when an accountable business owner understands the remaining exposure.
I identify personal, sensitive, confidential, and regulated data before designing processing flows.
I apply data minimization so systems collect and retain only what the purpose requires.
I define lawful and legitimate processing purposes before reusing personal data for new analytics or AI tasks.
I separate privacy obligations from general security controls because confidentiality alone does not establish lawful use.
I design consent, notice, rights handling, retention, deletion, correction, and access processes where they apply.
I reduce unnecessary data linkage, re-identification, and inference risk in analytics and AI workflows.
I distinguish anonymization from pseudonymization and validate whether re-identification remains reasonably possible.
I design cross-border and third-party data flows with jurisdictional and contractual constraints visible.
I apply privacy-by-design controls early enough that compliance does not become a late-stage retrofit.
I preserve evidence of privacy decisions, data flows, purposes, safeguards, and material exceptions.
I define incident severity from business consequence, scope, sensitivity, and operational impact rather than technical drama.
I design detection coverage around credible attack and abuse scenarios.
I establish accountable incident roles, decision rights, escalation paths, and communication channels before a crisis.
I preserve forensic evidence without unnecessarily delaying containment and recovery.
I distinguish containment, eradication, recovery, investigation, notification, and lessons learned as separate incident objectives.
I define when legal, privacy, executive, customer, insurer, regulator, or law-enforcement involvement may be required.
I prepare communication that is factual, timely, coordinated, and does not outrun verified evidence.
I test incident procedures with realistic scenarios rather than assuming documentation equals readiness.
I maintain out-of-band communication and access paths for incidents that compromise normal collaboration systems.
I convert incidents and near misses into control, architecture, training, and governance improvements.
I identify critical business activities and the maximum tolerable disruption before defining technology recovery targets.
I derive recovery time objectives from business consequence rather than selecting convenient technical numbers.
I derive recovery point objectives from acceptable data loss and transaction reconstruction capability.
I distinguish high availability, business continuity, disaster recovery, backup, and crisis management.
I define minimum viable business operations for degraded conditions rather than assuming full restoration is the only acceptable outcome.
I identify people, facilities, vendors, communications, data, credentials, and manual procedures required for continuity.
I design continuity strategies for regional, provider, workforce, cyber, physical, and dependency failures where material.
I make recovery priorities explicit so scarce resources are allocated deliberately during disruption.
I ensure continuity plans reflect real operating dependencies instead of isolated application inventories.
I revisit recovery objectives when product commitments, regulation, architecture, or business criticality changes.
I test restoration from backups instead of treating successful backup jobs as proof of recoverability.
I exercise failover, failback, degraded-mode, dependency-loss, and capacity scenarios appropriate to critical services.
I validate recovery under conditions where normal identity, network, communication, or administration paths are unavailable.
I test whether recovery procedures can be executed by realistic staff under time pressure.
I measure actual recovery performance against stated objectives and record gaps.
I include data integrity validation after recovery so restored systems do not silently resume with corrupted state.
I test shared failure modes that can defeat nominal redundancy.
I define rollback and recovery procedures for security-control and configuration changes that can disrupt operations.
I maintain disaster-recovery documentation, automation, credentials, and dependencies so they remain usable when needed.
I treat untested recovery assumptions as unresolved risk rather than completed controls.
I assess third parties according to the data, privilege, service criticality, and dependency they introduce.
I distinguish questionnaire completion from evidence that a supplier can meet required security and continuity obligations.
I define security, privacy, incident, audit, notification, data-return, deletion, and termination requirements in material contracts.
I identify concentration and correlated-failure risk across common cloud, identity, software, and service providers.
I govern software dependencies, packages, images, build systems, and update channels as supply-chain attack surfaces.
I evaluate cloud shared-responsibility boundaries so provider controls are not mistaken for customer responsibilities.
I require secure integration and credential practices for vendors with system or data access.
I define exit and continuity options when a critical provider is unavailable, compromised, acquired, or commercially changed.
I monitor material supplier changes and incidents instead of relying only on onboarding assessments.
I accept third-party residual risk explicitly when no practical alternative provides a better risk-adjusted outcome.
I define security policies as decision rules tied to material risk rather than collections of generic prohibitions.
I maintain evidence showing whether critical controls are designed, operating, and effective.
I distinguish compliance with a framework from actual resistance to the organization's credible threat scenarios.
I use vulnerabilities, incidents, audit findings, threat intelligence, and operational evidence to reprioritize controls.
I define accountable owners and due dates for material security and privacy remediation.
I track control exceptions with rationale, compensating controls, expiration, and review.
I measure security outcomes with indicators that reveal exposure, response, recovery, and control effectiveness rather than activity volume alone.
I train users and administrators around realistic behaviors and risks instead of treating annual completion as proof of competence.
I retire controls that create burden without reducing meaningful exposure and strengthen controls where evidence shows weakness.
I treat cybersecurity, privacy, and continuity as one continuously tested resilience capability rather than isolated compliance programs.
